resolution.note:
Both refuters killed every blocking finding, so the row stamps PASS:verify-refuted and this REVISE stays as the record. pedagogy §45 line 37: scope: The finding fails on scope lens (d), and the cited rule is not clearly binding on this surface.

What I checked:
- `check_pedagogy.md` §45 reads as the judge quoted it. It asks for "3 observable outcomes student exhibits on own codebase by next working day". Its examples are all engineer-side: worktree, test-before-fix, `CLAUDE.local.md`. Its only carve-out is arc-mood for M5/M6. It has no explicit exemption for Agents 101 openers.
- The rule's text and examples are AE101 engineer phrasing ("own codebase", "Monday"). This file is a non-code, manager-facing exercise. It has a 15-minute interview and `./challenge.md` as its only artefact.
- Convention across the Agents 101 training is no leap test:
  - Of the 18 exercises that `curriculum/trainings/agents-101/*.md` links, 13 have none (case-insensitive grep for 'leap test' or 'monday'). Only 5 have one.
  - The judge's "39 of 59" is a corpus-wide count dominated by AE101 files. I counted 40 of the 59 files matching 'leap' or 'monday' case-insensitively, so the number is roughly right but irrelevant to this training.
- The corpus's own judges have already ruled this a rule-scope question, not a per-file defect:
  - `build-for-the-gap.pedagogy.json` gives §45 N/A with the reason "Agents 101 exercises carry none by training convention... rule's 'own codebase' frame is engineer-side; filing it per file is the file-by-file fix the corpus avoids".
  - `build-for-the-gap.story.json` and `build-your-challenge-memory.story.json` also give N/A, and the latter names `name-your-challenge` and `personal-agent-homework` as siblings carrying no leap test.
  - `eval-loop.pedagogy.json` flags the same point as "a rule-scope question".
  - The `build-for-the-gap` pedagogy judge's notes say it is "one decision for the training" and should not be filed per file.
- This file's own audit line (L37-38) records pedagogy PASS at 2026-08-25. The file has not changed in a way that would invalidate that.
- The proposed fix would duplicate content the file already has. L53-55 give failure modes, escape hatches and a "one-sentence test". L60 states the artefact (`./challenge.md`). A leap test would restate that.
- The finding is marked "blocking", but it asserts only a corpus-wide convention gap. It names no student-visible harm from this file. A per-file block would apply an AE101-shaped rule to a body that was correct.

Caveats:
- There is no dated accept-note in this file pre-authorising the omission (lens c). I found the pedagogy-instance N/A rulings but no maintainer decision either way.
- If the maintainer wants §45 applied to Agents 101 at all, that is a training-level decision, not a blocking per-file finding on this file. / harm: Verified: grep -ci 'leap|monday' on name-your-challenge.md returns 0, and 39 of 59 exercise files do carry "Leap test". But the count is misleading. 17 of the 59 are apt101-* exercises and the rest are the engineer track. The judge's own "39 of 59" hides that Agents 101, the audience this exercise belongs to, mostly doesn't carry leap tests. Of the 18 exercises in the agents-101 training, only 4 have one (design-the-sharing-plan, personal-site-with-guardrails, share-your-work, test-the-sharing-plan). The 14 without include build-your-challenge-memory, eval-loop, three-minds-one-synthesis and hallucination-bakeoff. §45 is written for "own codebase by next working day" (engineer audience). This file's pedagogy verdict was PASS at the 2026-08-25 audit (@4d9c4af2) without one.

Harm: (a) Nobody in the room is worse off. This is a 15-minute opener, and its output, ./challenge.md, is immediately consumed in the same session by build-your-challenge-memory, which keys off it. A "Monday outcome" is not a meaningful horizon for an artifact used within the hour. The Role-in-Module-2 line and the View summary already name the artifact (a one-page challenge statement). The Deferred notes already carry the one-sentence test. (b) The harm statement ("nobody can tell whether it landed") restates §45 rather than showing a consequence. The file either exists and reads right, or it doesn't. (d) Other lines already carry the meaning, so the fix is largely a no-op. (c) Part of the proposed fix would break a claim. Item 2, "the decision the memory will serve is named", is not produced by name-your-challenge-1. That prompt asks only for the initiative, what's been tried, and where the student is stuck. Adding it would promise an outcome the exercise doesn't produce, which is the §45/§64 defect the compendium warns about. Item 3 (source list) lives only in scrollback.

Counter-evidence: §45 says "every exercise" with no explicit Agents 101 carve-out, and the leap test would sit in the maintainer block, so adding one costs little. The compendium's audit ledger also lists §45 as a confirmed gap on other files. If the maintainer wants uniform enforcement, a 2-item artefact-style leap test (challenge.md exists and passes the one-sentence test; scout list in scrollback) would be safe. As a BLOCKING finding, though, it does not survive the harm lens.; pedagogy §34 line 17: scope: The finding misreads L17 and overstates what rule §34 requires. Four points.

1. The judge's factual claim is wrong. It says L17 "names the floor (done work, self-improvement) but no ceiling." The L17 list is `last year's re-org`, `becoming a better leader`, `understanding AI`. Only the first is done work. `understanding AI` is an unbounded topic with no decision inside it, which is a too-wide case. `becoming a better leader` is open-ended in the same way. So L17 already names too-wide cases as "Not a fit". The Good example at L15 is also tightly bounded: a named decision, a pilot cohort and a sales briefing. §34's "bolded anti-pattern callout" form is not the only way to name a ceiling.

2. The student-side test the judge wants to add already exists in the pick step. Prompt `name-your-challenge-1` Q1 reads "In one sentence, what's the initiative? A real, midsized-to-large piece of work... scope, stakes, still open." The student's own Claude interviews them to a one-sentence scoped initiative. The "too-wide" failure is therefore caught in the same step. The judge's claim that a landfill memory results from a too-wide pick ignores this. L33 ("Scope matters most... landfill") sits at the end of the same short, 15-minute exercise.

3. §34 targets a different surface. Read at current wording, §34 covers task selection for agent execution. Its examples are "feature slice", "multi-file" and "30–60 min agent execution", and its placements are "prework + Phase 1 commit". This exercise picks a challenge to build a memory around. The analogy is loose. The judge is binding a coding-task-size rule to a different artifact. The rule's trigger is a maintainer-block "watch-for: too-big-task". The L53 watch-for is a facilitator redirect about a generic brief, which is a related but different failure mode.

4. The maintainer block shows prior review. Pedagogy was judged PASS at 4d9c4af2 on 2026-08-25. The one-sentence test is placed in "Deferred per student-facing-first rule" (L57-58) as a deliberate facilitator-side deferral. The room trainer is meant to run the 2-minute narrowing conversation (L53). The proposed fix would add student-facing body text, which would need a maintainer card under the approval gate. The harm is also low-dosage: the failure is recoverable, because the student sees the brief before saving and edits it ("Edit the brief if it doesn't sound like what keeps you up").

At most this is a stylistic placement preference (move the landfill line earlier), not a BLOCKING violation. I found no dated accept-note for this exact line, so point (c) of the scope lens does not apply. I could not run `rule.js`, because no such file exists in the core repo. I read §34 and §34b directly in `check_pedagogy.md` instead. / harm: Granting that §34 (name floor AND ceiling in task selection) reaches this exercise, the claimed harm does not hold.

(1) The ceiling is already carried, on the page and in the prompt the student runs next. L13 bounds the pick: "An initiative you own and work on in these weeks, one that produces work (memo, plan, decision, brief, campaign, rollout)". "In these weeks" and "produces work" cut out an open-ended theme such as "improve sales performance". L15's "Good" example is a specific, bounded initiative (Q2 pricing redesign, with a pilot cohort and a sales briefing), so it models the right width. That is a ceiling shown by example, which §34 allows. L33 ("a memory about 'our company' is a landfill") names the too-wide failure in the student's own vocabulary.

(2) The judge's "student-side one-sentence test" already exists. Prompt name-your-challenge-1 opens with "In one sentence, what's the initiative? A real, midsized-to-large piece of work... scope, stakes, still open." The agent interviews the student, so a too-wide answer gets probed there. It is also caught at the brief stage. L25 has the student edit the brief, and the maintainer block calls the source list a diagnostic for brief quality. The judge's claim that the ceiling cue only arrives after both prompts is therefore wrong. The prompt carries it before the brief is written. A too-wide pick does not silently produce a landfill.

(3) The defect is a deliberate deferral, not an omission. The maintainer block at L58 lists the "one-sentence test" and "too broad or too narrow" coaching under "Deferred per student-facing-first rule". The L53 watch-for also routes the generic brief to a trainer redirect and a 2-minute narrowing conversation. The judge's fix would pull a deliberately facilitator-side beat into the student body of a 15-minute exercise.

(4) The proposed fix costs more than it gains. It adds a second sentence to a deliberately terse pick step. Putting "improve sales performance" in the body also seeds the exact generic example the maintainer watches for. Because this is student-facing body text, any change would need a BEFORE/AFTER card under the §26 approval gate, which is a cost for a defect the prompt already covers.

(5) Verification: pedagogy PASS is stamped at 2026-08-25 on this body. The compendium file has no "§34" heading. Rule 34 is numbered "34." at line 91 of check_pedagogy.md, and it is scoped to agent-execution task selection. Its listed placements are prework and the Phase 1 commit, and this exercise is neither. Its "watch-for: too-big-task" trigger is not in this maintainer block, which has only a generic-brief watch-for. That watch-for is satisfied by the prompt's "one sentence" interview, so the rule's intent is met even if its letter applies.

No one in the room is worse off: the interview and the trainer catch the too-wide pick within the exercise's first minutes. The finding is tidiness, a restatement of the rule's wording rather than a consequence.
